Overall, government organisations have been more effective in addressing the compliance challenge, because only government can compel a recall and impose bans, backed by the ACCC's power to seek penalties. However, their effectiveness is limited by the partial recall. The best outcome would combine the ACCC's enforcement power with industry's technical knowledge and the speed of guidance, rather than relying on either body alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Four explicit criteria are set and each organisation is judged against them. The answer weighs the ACCC's enforcement power against the partial recall and the industry body's speed against its lack of legal force, and reaches an explicit judgement that the ACCC has been more effective, which is the evaluation the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Government can order recalls and ban unsafe goods, and the ACCC can seek penalties, so government has strong enforcement powers. The industry body issued voluntary guidance, which is quick and cooperative but has no legal force. Standards Australia standards are voluntary unless adopted into law. In the scenario, the recall covered only part of the stock and the guidance was two years old, which suggests both responses have been limited. Government is probably more effective than industry because it can enforce the law, but the government response has still been limited, so I think neither has been fully effective.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The roles and limits of both organisations are explained, and the scenario is used to show the limited responses. The evaluation is brief and the criteria are not set out, so the answer is in the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Government can order a recall. Industry bodies can issue guidance to their members.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One response from each organisation is identified with minimal evaluation. This is the 2-mark band.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A national inquiry finds that a popular brand of portable heater has repeatedly failed safety tests. The industry body issued voluntary guidance to its members two years earlier, and a responsible minister has since issued one recall notice that covered only part of the affected stock.

prompts.question: Account for the difficulty that industry organisations face in ensuring compliance with voluntary product safety standards.
markerNotes: Account for asks why. Each factor must be a reason the difficulty exists, not a description of what industry organisations do.
A useful distinction: an industry association may be able to remove a member from membership or withdraw endorsement, but it cannot impose fines or order a recall.
commonStudentErrors: Blaming industry bodies for non-compliance without explaining the structural reasons.
Saying voluntary standards are never followed. Many businesses comply, but without enforcement powers the non-compliant minority is hard to address.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Accounts for at least three factors, such as the absence of legal power to compel compliance, the cost of compliance for members, and the self-interest of member businesses, linking each factor to the difficulty of ensuring compliance
3 marks: Accounts for two factors with accurate explanation
2 marks: Accounts for one factor with some explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about compliance difficulties

sampleAnswers.answer: Industry organisations face several difficulties in ensuring compliance with voluntary standards. The first is the absence of enforcement powers: voluntary standards are not legally binding, so an industry organisation cannot impose fines or order a recall, and removing a member is a weak sanction against a business that does not depend on membership. The second is cost, as compliance requires testing and manufacturing changes that a business may avoid when the standard is not required by law. The third is self-interest, because organisations funded by the businesses they represent may be reluctant to take firm action against members.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three factors are accounted for, the lack of enforcement powers, the cost of compliance and the self-interest of funding members, and each is linked to the difficulty of ensuring compliance. This reaches the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Voluntary standards have no legal force, so industry organisations cannot fine businesses. They can only remove members, which is a weak penalty for businesses that do not need membership.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One factor, the absence of enforcement powers, is accounted for with some explanation. A second factor is needed for the 3-mark band.

dotPoints.description: Responses to non-compliance with industry standards and product safety, including enforcement measures

prompts.question: Explain how the law responds to non-compliance with industry standards and product safety requirements, including the enforcement measures available.
markerNotes: Group responses by purpose: stopping the unsafe product (bans), removing it from homes (mandatory recalls), punishing the breach (penalties), and compensating those harmed (consumer remedies). Full marks link each one to the scenario.
The written warning matters. Continuing to sell after a written warning is conduct a court is likely to view as more culpable when it sets penalties, and this should feature in the application.
commonStudentErrors: Describing recalls as voluntary without explaining that a mandatory recall can be ordered under the law.
Forgetting the consumers who already bought the product. The remedies for them are part of the answer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains at least two responses, such as product bans, mandatory recalls and penalties imposed by court orders, explains the purpose of each, applies at least one to the manufacturer in the scenario, and identifies how the law protects consumers who have already bought the product
5 marks: Explains two responses accurately and applies at least one to the scenario
4 marks: Explains two responses accurately, with limited application to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one response accurately
2 marks: Identifies a response with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that the law penalises unsafe products

sampleAnswers.answer:
When a manufacturer's non-compliance with a product safety requirement occurs, the law provides enforcement measures with different purposes. The first is product bans. A responsible minister can ban a product that does not meet a mandatory standard or presents a safety risk, which stops the manufacturer selling it. In the scenario, a ban would stop the continued sale of the children's product despite the written warning. The second is mandatory recalls. Where a product is already in homes, a responsible minister can order a compulsory recall, removing the product from consumers. The loose parts and choking risk for young children show why this matters, because the danger is present in products already sold.

The third is penalties imposed by court orders. The ACCC can take the manufacturer to court for civil penalties, which punish the breach and deter other suppliers from ignoring warnings. Continuing to sell after a written warning is likely to weigh against the manufacturer when penalties are set. The fourth is consumer remedies. Consumers who bought the product may be entitled to a refund, a replacement or compensation for injury, and may rely on the consumer guarantees.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Product bans, mandatory recalls, court-ordered penalties and consumer remedies are each explained by their purpose and applied to the manufacturer's continued sales and the children's product. The answer also protects the consumers who already bought it, which earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A responsible minister can ban unsafe products, which would stop the manufacturer selling the product in the scenario. A mandatory recall can require the supplier to remove products already sold, which matters because the parts are coming loose. The ACCC can also take the manufacturer to court for penalties. Consumers who bought the product may also be able to claim a refund.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two responses, product bans and mandatory recalls, are explained with some application to the children's product, and penalties and consumer remedies are noted briefly. The purposes are not developed and the warning is not used, so the answer is in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The law punishes companies that sell unsafe products.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement that unsafe products are penalised, with no specific response identified. It earns the single mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A manufacturer continues to sell a children's product that does not meet a mandatory safety standard, even after the ACCC has warned it in writing. Some consumers report that parts come loose and create a choking risk for young children.

prompts.question: Identify two enforcement measures that can be used against a supplier that sells unsafe products.
markerNotes: Identify asks for named items. Name each measure precisely, because a general description such as 'the ACCC can punish suppliers' earns no mark.
Two different measures are needed, not two versions of the same action.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a measure that belongs to a different regulator, such as ASIC's banning orders for credit providers.
Naming the Australian Financial Complaints Authority as a product safety measure. It resolves individual financial complaints and has no power to ban or recall goods.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct enforcement measures, such as a product ban, a mandatory recall, or court-ordered penalties
1 mark: Identifies one enforcement measure without further explanation

sampleAnswers.answer: Two enforcement measures for unsafe products are product bans, where a responsible minister prohibits supply, and mandatory recalls, where a minister orders the supplier to recall products already with consumers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct enforcement measures, product bans and mandatory recalls, are identified and briefly explained, which earns both marks. The answer stays focused on the two measures the question asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: A responsible minister can ban a product from being sold.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One enforcement measure is identified without further detail. It earns the single mark.

dotPoints.description: The need for competition in the marketplace

prompts.question: Explain why competition in the marketplace is needed to protect consumers.
markerNotes: Explain the need by linking competition to consumer outcomes: prices, choice, quality and innovation. Then show what happens when competition is weakened.
Use the scenario. Reducing the number of competitors is how market power grows, which is why the need for competition is a legal issue as well as an economic one.
commonStudentErrors: Saying competition is good without explaining the outcomes it produces for consumers.
Treating the scenario as only a merger problem, without explaining the general need for competition.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains at least two reasons competition is needed, such as lower prices, greater choice, innovation and the constraint of market power, applies them to the town in the scenario, and explains why competition must be protected by law
5 marks: Explains two reasons accurately and applies at least one to the scenario
4 marks: Explains two reasons accurately, with limited application to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one reason accurately, without application
2 marks: Identifies a reason with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that competition is good

sampleAnswers.answer:
Competition is needed in the marketplace because it constrains the power of businesses over consumers. When several businesses compete for customers, each has an incentive to lower prices, improve quality and offer greater choice, because customers can take their money elsewhere. Competition also encourages innovation, as businesses seek to win customers.

The scenario shows what happens when competition is reduced. When one supermarket chain takes over the town's only independent competitor, the remaining supermarkets are no longer constrained by a rival, and they raise prices. Residents cannot easily avoid the increase by shopping elsewhere, so the businesses exercise market power. Market power is the ability of a business to raise prices without losing customers to competitors.

Because the loss of competition harms consumers directly, the law protects competition rather than leaving it to market forces alone. The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) prohibits conduct that substantially lessens competition, such as anti-competitive agreements and certain acquisitions. Competition is therefore needed both as a source of consumer benefits and as a legal safeguard against the abuse of market power.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Lower prices, greater choice and innovation are explained as consumer benefits, and the scenario is used to show what happens when competition is lost. The answer then explains why the law must protect competition, which is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition means businesses compete for customers. This leads to lower prices and better choice for consumers, because customers can switch to another business. In the scenario, the supermarkets raised prices after a competitor was taken over, because they had less competition. This shows that without competition, businesses can raise prices and consumers have fewer options.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two reasons, lower prices and choice, are explained accurately, with limited application to the town. The protective role of the law and the idea of market power are not developed, so the answer is in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition is good for people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement that competition is good, with no reason explained. It earns the single mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two supermarket chains in a regional town both raise prices after one takes over the town's only independent competitor. Residents complain that there is no longer any real choice about where to shop.

prompts.question: State two benefits of competition for consumers in a market.
markerNotes: State is brief. Two benefits, each short and accurate, are enough.
Name a benefit to the consumer. A business gaining more customers or more profit is not a consumer benefit.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a benefit to businesses, such as growth or profit, rather than a benefit to consumers.
Stating the same benefit twice in different words, such as 'cheaper' and 'lower prices'.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: States two accurate benefits, such as lower prices, greater choice, better quality or more innovation
1 mark: States one accurate benefit

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition benefits consumers in two main ways. First, lower prices, because businesses compete to attract customers. Second, greater choice, innovation and quality, as businesses that want to win customers offer wider ranges and better products.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct consumer benefits are stated, lower prices and greater choice, innovation and quality, each with a brief reason. Both are gains for consumers, which the question requires, so this earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition means lower prices for people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One accurate benefit is stated without elaboration. A second, distinct benefit is needed for full marks.

dotPoints.description: The regulation of competition in Australia

prompts.question: Describe how the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) regulates competition in Australia.
markerNotes: Describe the prohibitions in plain terms: what conduct is prohibited and what makes it unlawful.
Full marks name the regulator and the enforcement route, such as civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court and criminal prosecution for cartel conduct.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the Act regulates prices. It regulates conduct that harms competition; it does not set prices.
Confusing the Competition and Consumer Act with the Australian Consumer Law. The ACL is Schedule 2 to the Act and deals mainly with consumer protection.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes at least three prohibitions in the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), such as misuse of market power, exclusive dealing, cartel conduct and anti-competitive mergers, and identifies the ACCC as the regulator that enforces them
3 marks: Describes two prohibitions accurately and identifies the regulator, or describes three prohibitions with limited accuracy
2 marks: Describes one prohibition, or the regulator, in general terms
1 mark: Identifies the Competition and Consumer Act without describing how it regulates competition

sampleAnswers.answer: The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) regulates competition by prohibiting harmful conduct. Part IV prohibits anti-competitive agreements and cartel conduct, such as agreements to fix prices, and cartel conduct is a criminal offence and a civil contravention. The Act also prohibits the misuse of market power, where a business with substantial market power engages in conduct with the purpose, or the effect, of substantially lessening competition, such as eliminating a rival. Exclusive dealing is also prohibited where it substantially lessens competition. From 1 January 2026, mergers and acquisitions that meet the notification thresholds must be notified to the ACCC and cannot proceed until it determines they may. The ACCC enforces these prohibitions through investigation and Federal Court action.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Four prohibitions are described, cartel conduct, misuse of market power, exclusive dealing and mergers, each in terms of what makes the conduct unlawful, and the ACCC's enforcement route is identified. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Competition and Consumer Act prohibits businesses from misusing market power, which means a large business cannot use its power to push out competitors. The ACCC enforces the Act.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One prohibition is described with an explanation, and the regulator is identified in general terms. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 deals with competition in Australia.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The Act is identified without describing how it regulates competition. It earns the single mark.

prompts.question: Clarify the role of the ACCC in regulating competition, using the scenario.
markerNotes: Clarify means making the role clear and specific. The ACCC investigates, enforces and reviews. Name each function and tie it to the facts.
The petrol stations are a price-fixing scenario. Top answers note that a secret price agreement is cartel conduct, and that the ACCC can seek penalties and refer criminal conduct for prosecution.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the ACCC as the court. It investigates and takes action, but the Federal Court decides whether a contravention has occurred and orders penalties.
Saying the ACCC sets petrol prices. Competition law prohibits agreements between competitors, but it does not set prices.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies at least three functions of the ACCC, such as investigating suspected cartel conduct, taking civil action in the Federal Court and reviewing mergers, applying them to the petrol stations in the scenario
2 marks: Clarifies two functions of the ACCC accurately

sampleAnswers.answer: The ACCC is the regulator that enforces competition law. In the scenario, it would investigate whether the two petrol stations have reached a secret price agreement, which is cartel conduct under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010. If the evidence supports it, the ACCC can take civil action in the Federal Court for penalties, or refer the conduct for criminal prosecution. The ACCC also reviews mergers, but here its role is to investigate and enforce, not set prices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The ACCC's investigation and civil action in the Federal Court are applied to the petrol stations, and the answer clarifies that its role is to enforce rather than set prices. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ACCC investigates suspected cartel conduct. It can take the petrol stations to the Federal Court for penalties.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two functions are clarified accurately and applied to the scenario. A third function, such as merger review, is needed for full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ACCC is the regulator for competition in Australia.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The ACCC is identified as the regulator without any function being clarified. It earns the single mark.

dotPoints.description: Challenges for consumers due to anti-competitive behaviour, including limits on choice and price increases

prompts.question: Analyse the challenges for consumers caused by anti-competitive behaviour, including limits on choice and price increases, in a market like the one in the scenario.
markerNotes: Analyse means showing how one thing leads to another. Trace the chain from collusion or market power to higher prices and fewer options, and then to the effect on particular consumers.
The scenario shows a pattern (simultaneous price rises and exit of rivals) that suggests collusion. Top answers say the pattern requires investigation rather than treating it as proof.
Detection is a challenge in its own right. Secret agreements are hard to prove, and consumers cannot see why prices change.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the petrol stations are guilty of collusion. Parallel price rises alone do not prove an agreement, so the answer should say the conduct requires investigation.
Describing the effects on consumers without linking them to the conduct that caused them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Analyses how anti-competitive behaviour, including collusion and misuse of market power, causes limits on choice and price increases for consumers, draws out the consequences for different consumers in the scenario, and explains why these challenges are hard to detect or remedy
5-6 marks: Analyses the link between anti-competitive behaviour and consumer harm, with accurate legal and economic reference applied to the scenario, though some consequences are not drawn out
3-4 marks: Explains anti-competitive behaviour and at least one challenge for consumers, with limited analysis or application
1-2 marks: Identifies a challenge for consumers with minimal explanation

sampleAnswers.answer: Anti-competitive behaviour creates several challenges for consumers, and the scenario shows how these challenges reinforce each other. The first is collusion. The petrol stations raising prices at the same time may be coordinating, which would be cartel conduct if they reached an agreement about price. Parallel price rises alone do not prove an agreement, but the pattern suggests that an investigation is needed. The second challenge is market power. When rivals exit the market, the remaining business gains greater market power, and it can raise prices without losing customers to a nearby competitor. Within two years, the town has only one independent station, so the power to set prices has effectively passed to a single business. The third challenge is limits on choice. Residents who cannot drive far have no realistic alternative, so they must accept the price or go without fuel. This is a particular problem for people in regional areas, older people and those on low incomes, who have fewer options and less capacity to absorb higher prices. The fourth challenge is the price increases themselves, which reduce the money consumers have for other goods and services. Because the increases are gradual, consumers may not recognise that competition has been reduced until the price is already much higher. The final challenge is detection. Secret agreements between competitors are hard to find, and consumers have no visibility into whether prices are set competitively or through coordination. The ACCC must investigate, gather evidence and prove the conduct, which takes time, and by the time a case is resolved the market may have changed. These challenges show why anti-competitive behaviour harms consumers in a way that is cumulative and hard to reverse. Once competitors have exited, consumers cannot simply return to earlier prices, because the market structure has changed. The analysis therefore shows that the harm is not only the immediate price increase, but the long-term loss of competitive pressure on the town's businesses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Five linked challenges are analysed: collusion, market power, limits on choice, price increases and detection. Each is traced to the petrol stations and the consequences for particular consumers are drawn out. The answer ends with the cumulative and irreversible nature of the harm, which is the analysis the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Anti-competitive behaviour such as collusion can lead to higher prices. When the petrol stations raise prices together, consumers pay more and have less choice. In the scenario, the number of stations has fallen from three to one, so the remaining station has market power. Consumers in the town have limited alternatives, particularly those who cannot drive far. Price increases reduce what consumers can afford. It is also hard to prove a secret agreement, so the ACCC would need to investigate. Overall, consumers are harmed because competition has been reduced, although the law can respond.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The link between collusion, market power and consumer harm is explained and applied to the scenario, and detection is noted. Some consequences, such as the effect on particular groups and the irreversibility of the harm, are not drawn out, so the answer is in the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Consumers pay higher prices when petrol stations do not compete. There may be fewer choices for people in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two challenges are identified with minimal explanation. This is the 1-2 band, and a fuller explanation of the link would be needed for more marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A consumer in a competitive market and one in a market dominated by a single supplier are in very different positions. In the first town, four providers compete, so each has an incentive to keep prices low, because a customer who finds a better offer can switch. Consumers in the competitive market gain lower prices and innovation, while those in the dominated market face higher prices and limits on choice.

dotPoints.description: Responses to anti-competitive behaviour, including enforcement measures

prompts.question: Explain how the law responds to anti-competitive behaviour, including the enforcement measures available to the ACCC and to affected parties.
markerNotes: Group the responses by who brings them and what they achieve: ACCC enforcement (penalties and orders), criminal prosecution for cartels, and private damages actions for those harmed.
Apply the response to the conduct. Exclusive dealing is a different wrong from cartel conduct, so the best answers choose the response that fits the retailer's conduct.
commonStudentErrors: Listing every remedy without choosing the response that fits the conduct in the scenario.
Saying cartel offences apply to the retailer. The scenario describes exclusive dealing, which is a separate prohibition.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains at least two responses, such as civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court, criminal prosecution for serious cartel conduct, court orders and private damages actions, applies at least one to the retailer's conduct, and explains the purpose of each response
5 marks: Explains two responses accurately with reference to the ACCC's powers, and applies at least one to the scenario
4 marks: Explains two responses accurately, with limited application to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one response accurately
2 marks: Identifies a response with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that anti-competitive behaviour is illegal

sampleAnswers.answer:
The law responds to anti-competitive behaviour through several enforcement measures: ACCC enforcement, criminal prosecution in serious cases and private actions by those harmed. The ACCC can investigate conduct and bring civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), seeking penalties and orders that stop the conduct. In the scenario, the retailer's requirement that suppliers stop supplying competing retailers is likely to be exclusive dealing, which is prohibited where it substantially lessens competition. The ACCC could seek penalties and orders requiring the retailer to stop imposing these conditions.

Serious cartel conduct, such as agreements between competitors to fix prices, is treated differently. It is a criminal offence that can be prosecuted by the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, carrying the risk of imprisonment for individuals. Finally, a business harmed by anti-competitive conduct may bring a private action for damages, so competitors and suppliers can recover their losses. The choice between responses depends on the conduct, and exclusive dealing is usually addressed through ACCC proceedings rather than criminal prosecution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Civil penalties and court orders, criminal prosecution for cartel offences and private damages are explained by their purpose. The exclusive dealing conduct in the scenario is identified and the response that fits it is applied, which places the answer in the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ACCC can take a business to the Federal Court for conduct that breaches the Competition and Consumer Act, and the court can impose penalties. In the scenario, the retailer's conditions on suppliers may be exclusive dealing, so the ACCC could seek penalties. Businesses that have been harmed can also sue for damages.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two responses, civil penalties and private damages, are explained, with limited application to the retailer's exclusive dealing. The purpose of each response and the court orders are not developed, so the answer is in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Anti-competitive behaviour is against the law.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement that the conduct is illegal, with no response explained. It earns the single mark.

markerNotes: Predict means forecast from the evidence. The internal email is direct evidence of an agreement, which makes enforcement more likely and more serious.

dotPoints.description: The evolving concept of family in Australia

prompts.question: Explain the evolving concept of family in Australia, using the scenario.
markerNotes: Explain the change and the legal response together. The family has become more diverse, and the law has been amended or interpreted to recognise that diversity.
Apply the change to the scenario. Each relationship in the family should be matched to a legal recognition, such as de facto status under the Family Law Act or same-sex marriage.
commonStudentErrors: Describing family types without linking them to changes in the law.
Saying same-sex couples can now marry without naming the amending legislation or when it took effect.
keywords: Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains at least two ways the concept of family has changed, such as the recognition of de facto relationships, same-sex marriage, and blended or kinship families, links each change to the law, and applies them to the family in the scenario
5 marks: Explains two changes accurately with reference to legal recognition, and applies at least one to the scenario
4 marks: Explains two changes accurately, with limited application to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one change accurately, without application
2 marks: Identifies a change with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that families are changing

sampleAnswers.answer:
The evolving concept of family in Australia reflects changes in how families are structured and how the law responds to them. Traditionally, the family was understood as a married couple with children. Today, families include de facto couples, same-sex couples, blended families and kinship arrangements.

The family in the scenario shows several of these changes. The same-sex couple raising two children from one partner's previous relationship is a blended family. The Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 (Cth) changed the definition of marriage to the union of two people, allowing same-sex couples to marry from 9 December 2017. Before this, they could not marry under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth).

The adult son and his partner are in a de facto relationship. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) allows de facto couples to seek property settlement and maintenance on separation, provided the relationship meets the statutory test, such as living together for at least two years. The grandmother's care of the children reflects kinship, which the law recognises through child protection placement rules.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three changes are explained, the recognition of same-sex marriage, de facto relationships and kinship care, each linked to specific legislation and applied to the family in the scenario. The answer shows how the law has moved from a single model of family to recognising a range of relationships, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Families in Australia are more diverse than they used to be. De facto couples, same-sex couples and blended families are all common. The law has changed to recognise some of these relationships, such as same-sex marriage in 2017. In the scenario, the adult son and his partner are in a de facto relationship, which the Family Law Act recognises for property matters if the relationship lasts at least two years. The grandmother caring for the children is a kinship arrangement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two changes are explained accurately, same-sex marriage and de facto recognition, with some application to the family. The application is limited to labelling each relationship, and the blended family and kinship points are not linked to the law, so the answer sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Families are changing in Australia and the law has changed to match.

prompts.question: Assess the interrelationship between changing community values and the achievement of just outcomes for families. In your answer, you must refer to at least ONE contemporary issue.
markerNotes: The top answer shows how a specific change in the concept of family, such as the recognition of de facto couples or same-sex marriage, has changed the legal outcomes for families, and then assesses whether those outcomes are just.
The contemporary issue must test the relationship, for example by asking whether the law's understanding of family now protects members who fall outside it.
Kinship care and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander concept of family show that community values differ between groups, and an answer that recognises this is more sustained.
commonStudentErrors: Lists changes in the concept of family without connecting them to outcomes for family members.
Presents the change to same-sex marriage as a change in values alone, without showing the legal change it produced.
Treats the best interests principle as always achieving just outcomes, without considering families harmed by the process.
prompts.markingCriteria:
21-25 marks: Demonstrates extensive understanding of community values and just outcomes relating to family law; Makes an informed judgement about interrelationship between changing community values and achievement of just outcomes for families; Integrates relevant examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents AND at least ONE contemporary issue; Presents a sustained, logical and cohesive response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
16-20 marks: Demonstrates substantial understanding of community values and just outcomes relating to family law; Makes a sound judgement about the interrelationship between changing community values and achievement of just outcomes for families; Uses relevant examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents AND at least ONE contemporary issue; Presents a logical and cohesive response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
11-15 marks: Demonstrates an understanding of community values and just outcomes relating to family law; Makes some judgement about the interrelationship between changing community values and achievement of just outcomes for families; Makes some reference to examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents AND at least ONE contemporary issue; Presents a structured response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
6-10 marks: Demonstrates limited understanding of community values and just outcomes relating to family law; Makes statements about the interrelationship between changing community values and achievement of just outcomes for families; Makes limited reference to examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents AND may refer to a contemporary issue; Uses some relevant legal terminology
1-5 marks: Writes in general terms about the law relating to families; May include reference to legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; May refer to general legal terms

sampleAnswers.answer:
Changing community values about the family have reshaped family law in Australia, and the interrelationship with just outcomes is real but uneven. The law now recognises a wider range of families than it once did, which has increased fairness for many people. However, the same law can still leave some family members without protection, particularly where violence or separation is involved.

The concept of family has changed considerably. Community acceptance of de facto relationships led to the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) being extended to de facto couples, so that couples who had never married could seek property settlement and parenting orders. The Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 (Cth) changed the definition of marriage to allow same-sex couples to marry, reflecting a major shift in community values. These changes show the law moving from a single model of the family towards one that recognises the relationships people actually form.

Those changes have improved just outcomes for many families. A de facto partner who contributed to a relationship can now seek a property settlement, and a same-sex couple can marry and have the relationship recognised in the same way as other couples. Since the Family Law Amendment Act 2023 took effect in May 2024, the Act no longer presumes equal shared parental responsibility: parenting orders turn on the best interests of the child, so a parent's relationship with a child is considered on its merits rather than by the parents' marital status. The law therefore reflects values of equality and fairness more closely than before.

Just outcomes are not guaranteed, however. Family violence remains a serious problem, and a family member who is controlled or harmed in a relationship that the law does not recognise, or who fears the process, may not get the protection the community expects. Kinship care and family structures for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples show a different concept of family. Legal forms built around the nuclear family do not always reflect kinship obligations, and this can produce outcomes that fail some communities.

A contemporary issue is technology-facilitated family violence, in which a partner uses phones, social media or tracking to control or threaten a family member. The community now expects the law to protect against this, and state orders such as apprehended domestic violence orders can restrict electronic contact. Yet the evidence is digital, the abuse can cross state and national borders, and courts must apply the best interests principle while the family may still be in danger. This tests whether the law's changing understanding of family is matched by effective outcomes.

The interrelationship is therefore strong where values have led to recognition, and weaker where recognition has not translated into protection. The law's changing concept of family has increased fairness for couples and parents. But the best interests principle, applied to families affected by violence, can produce outcomes that the community would not regard as just, if a child remains at risk because a court has relied on contact arrangements.

Overall, changing community values have reshaped family law towards greater recognition and equality, and this has improved outcomes for many families. The achievement of just outcomes is less certain where violence, kinship and digital abuse fall outside the model of family the law was built around. The relationship between changing values and just outcomes is therefore close in the recognition of families, but less close in protecting every family member.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21-25 row by linking a specific change in the concept of family, such as de facto recognition and same-sex marriage, to outcomes for families, and by testing the link against technology-facilitated family violence. A sharper treatment of kinship and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander family structures would deepen the assessment.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Changing community values have changed the concept of family in Australian law, and this has affected whether families receive just outcomes. The relationship is real but uneven, because the law has widened recognition more quickly than it has protected every family member.

The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) now covers de facto couples, following community acceptance of de facto relationships. A de facto partner can seek a property settlement and parenting orders in the same way as a married spouse. The Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 (Cth) allowed same-sex couples to marry, which reflected a major shift in community values. These changes show the law responding to what the community accepts as a family.

These changes help achieve just outcomes. A de facto partner who contributed to a relationship can now seek a property settlement, and same-sex couples can marry on the same footing as other couples. The best interests principle applies to all families, so a child's relationship with each parent is considered on its merits.

However, the law does not always produce just outcomes. Family violence is a contemporary issue and remains a serious problem. A family member who fears the process, or who is harmed in a relationship the law does not recognise, may not get the protection the community expects. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families may have kinship arrangements that the law does not always recognise.

Overall, changing values have led to a fairer law, but the relationship between values and outcomes is not perfect. The law has become fairer, but protection for every family member is not yet achieved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 11–15 row by making some judgement about the interrelationship, with reference to the de facto and same-sex marriage changes and to family violence as a contemporary issue. Stating that values and outcomes both changed, without explaining how one produced the other, keeps it below the 16–20 row. Explaining how a specific change in values produced a specific outcome would lift it. The phrase ‘The law has become fairer’ shows the judgement is still broad.

sampleAnswers.answer: The concept of family in Australia has changed, and the law now recognises de facto couples and same-sex marriage. These changes help families. Some families still face problems with the law.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-5 row by describing changes to family law in general terms, without assessing how they relate to just outcomes. Connecting one change in values to one outcome for families would lift it to the 6-10 row.

dotPoints.description: Principles of the family law system

prompts.question: Describe the principles of the family law system in Australia.
markerNotes: Describe the principles in the Family Law Act rather than general values. The paramountcy of the child's best interests and the consideration of the child's relationship with both parents where it is safe are the core statutory principles.
Full marks show how the principles fit together: the child's relationship with both parents is protected, but not at the expense of safety.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the court gives custody to one parent. The Family Law Act uses parenting orders and parental responsibility, and asks what is in the child's best interests.
Describing the principles without naming the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth).
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the principle that the best interests of the child are the paramount consideration, the benefit to children of a relationship with both parents where it is safe, parental responsibility without any presumption of equal shared responsibility, and the protection of family members from harm, including family violence, using accurate terms
3 marks: Describes three principles with limited accuracy or detail
2 marks: Describes two principles in general terms
1 mark: Identifies one principle without description

sampleAnswers.answer: The family law system in Australia is governed by the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), which sets out principles. The most important is that the best interests of the child are the paramount consideration in parenting decisions. Courts consider factors such as the child's relationship with each parent, the child's views where appropriate, and the risk of harm or family violence. A second principle is the benefit to the child of a relationship with both parents, where it is safe to do so. The Act also protects family members from harm, recognising family violence, allowing protective orders and encouraging family dispute resolution before court. Together, these principles aim to protect children while keeping them connected to both parents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The best interests paramountcy, the benefit of a relationship with both parents where safe, and the protection of family members are described, with the factors courts weigh. The answer shows how the principles operate together, which the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Family Law Act says the best interests of the child come first. Children should have a relationship with both parents where it is safe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two principles are described in general terms, without the benefit of a relationship with both parents or the protection of family members. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Family law aims to protect families.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general aim is stated rather than a principle described. It earns the single mark.

prompts.question: Apply the best interests of the child principle under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) to the disagreement between Mia and Jordan.
markerNotes: Apply means weigh the facts against the principle. Name each factor and link it to the child's best interests, rather than stating a conclusion.
The principle does not decide the outcome automatically. There is no presumption of equal shared parental responsibility, so the court weighs the child's best interests.
Top answers mention family dispute resolution as the usual first step before parenting orders are sought, which is a practical point the question invites.
commonStudentErrors: Deciding the outcome on the basis of which parent is the better parent. The test is the child's best interests, not the merits of the parents.
Treating the grandparents' involvement as irrelevant. Relationships with other significant people can be relevant to the child's welfare.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the best interests of the child principle to the disagreement, weighs the relevant factors in the scenario such as the child's relationship with each parent, stability and the grandparents' involvement, reaches a supported conclusion, and explains the role of parental responsibility and dispute resolution
4 marks: Applies the best interests principle to the scenario with a supported conclusion, but with limited explanation of the factors or of parental responsibility
3 marks: Identifies the best interests principle and applies it to the scenario in general terms
2 marks: Identifies the principle with minimal application to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about children's welfare

sampleAnswers.answer:
The best interests of the child are the paramount consideration under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), so the court begins with the child's interests, not the parents' preferences. Jordan's wish is supported by the grandparents' nearby involvement, a relevant relationship for the child. Mia's evidence that the child is settled at home goes to stability and routine. The court would weigh the benefit of a relationship with both parents, if safe, against these factors and any risk of harm.

Parental responsibility is a separate question from where the child lives, and parenting orders address both by reference to the child's best interests. A balanced arrangement that keeps the child settled at school while maintaining a substantial relationship with Jordan is most consistent with those interests. The parents should attend family dispute resolution before applying for parenting orders, unless an exception applies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The best interests principle is applied to the competing factors, the grandparents' relationships and the child's stability, and the role of parental responsibility is explained. The answer reaches a supported conclusion and adds family dispute resolution as the practical next step, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The best interests of the child are the paramount consideration in the Family Law Act. The court would consider the child's relationship with both parents and with the grandparents. Jordan wants the child to spend most school weeks with him, and Mia says the child's routine should stay the same. The court would decide what is best for the child, and the parents should try family dispute resolution first.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The principle is identified and applied to the parents' positions in general terms. The factors are listed rather than weighed, and the role of parental responsibility is not explained, so the answer is in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The child should have the best outcome for their wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement about children's welfare, with no principle applied to the scenario. It earns the single mark.

dotPoints.description: The need to regulate family relationships and protect family members

prompts.question: Explain the need to regulate family relationships and protect family members, using the scenario.
markerNotes: Explain the need by naming the risk to the family member (violence, neglect or exploitation) and the legal response that addresses it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The need to regulate family relationships arises because vulnerable people can be harmed within the household, so the law must protect family members. Children and older people depend on others for care, so the law must set obligations for carers and provide protection where they are breached. In the scenario, the 15-year-old is vulnerable because of her age and the repeated threats against her, which create a risk of family violence. Protective orders, such as an apprehended domestic violence order under New South Wales law, could be sought against the partner. The school's safety concerns also point to child protection involvement. Dispute resolution may be inappropriate where violence is present, as the law makes exceptions for family violence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two reasons, the protection of a vulnerable young person from family violence and the need for clear care obligations, are explained and applied to the scenario. The answer links each to a legal mechanism, including protective orders and child protection, which places it in the top band.

sampleAnswers.feedback: One reason is explained accurately, but it is not applied to the young person in the scenario. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement that families need protection, with no reason explained. It earns the single mark.

prompts.question: Justify the view that the law should regulate family relationships, including marriage and de facto relationships, to protect vulnerable family members.
markerNotes: Justify means give reasons for a position and answer the strongest counter-argument. A position with no reasons earns little, and a list of reasons with no position does not reach the top band.
The strongest reasons link the law to the protection of vulnerable people. The family law system and state protection orders exist for that purpose, not to control private choices.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a balanced description of both views and never reaching a position.
Justifying regulation in general terms, without showing which vulnerable members it protects and how.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a clear position on the extent of legal regulation, supported by at least two reasons such as the protection of vulnerable members from family violence and the clarity of rights and obligations for couples, addresses the opposing argument about private life, and reaches a supported conclusion
5 marks: Justifies a position with two accurate reasons and some reference to the opposing view
4 marks: Justifies a position with two reasons, with limited reference to the opposing view
3 marks: Gives one reason in support of a position
2 marks: Makes a statement of position with minimal reasoning

sampleAnswers.answer:
The law should regulate family relationships to a significant degree, because family life is not purely private when vulnerable family members are at risk of harm. The first reason is protection. Children, older people and people with disability cannot always protect themselves. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) makes the child's best interests paramount, and state protective orders, such as apprehended domestic violence orders, give remedies against threats of violence. Without regulation, these members would have no formal remedy.

The second reason is clarity. Formal rules about marriage and de facto relationships tell couples how property, maintenance and parenting will be dealt with on separation. Without this clarity, the weaker party may be left with little protection, particularly where one partner controls the finances.

Opponents argue that governments should not intervene in private life, which has force for adults making consenting choices. However, this does not answer the case for protecting people who cannot protect themselves. The law can respect private life by limiting intervention to cases of harm, dependency or unfairness. In my view, regulation is justified where it protects vulnerable members and provides clarity, but it should be targeted rather than universal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The position is clear, supported by two reasons (the protection of vulnerable family members and the clarity that formal rules give couples), and the opposing argument about private life is answered by limiting state intervention to cases of harm. The conclusion that regulation should be targeted follows from the reasons, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The law should protect vulnerable family members, such as children, because they cannot always protect themselves. Family law gives clear rules about property and parenting after separation, which helps both parties. Some people say the government should not interfere in private life, but the law only interferes where people are at risk. Overall, I think regulation is justified to protect people, but it should not control all family choices.

prompts.question: ‘Non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of the law.’ To what extent is this statement accurate in relation to families?
markerNotes: The top answer makes a judgement on whether non-compliance with orders and protections limits the law, and separates parenting orders, child support and family violence orders, which have different enforcement problems.
A strong answer treats the best interests principle and family dispute resolution as the law's responses, then shows where they fail when a party does not comply.
Examples should name the specific legal tool, such as an apprehended domestic violence order or a parenting order, and show how a breach is treated.
commonStudentErrors: Describes family law in general, such as the Family Law Act, without judging whether non-compliance challenges its effectiveness.
Treats all family law orders as equally enforced, without distinguishing child support, parenting orders and family violence orders.
Assumes the best interests principle always works, without considering what happens when a parent does not comply.
prompts.markingCriteria:
21-25 marks: Demonstrates extensive understanding of the law concerning families; Makes an informed judgement about the extent to which non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of the law; Integrates relevant examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; Presents a sustained, logical and cohesive response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
16-20 marks: Demonstrates substantial understanding of the law concerning families; Makes a sound judgement about the extent to which non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of the law; Uses relevant examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; Presents a logical and cohesive response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
11-15 marks: Demonstrates an understanding of the law concerning families; Makes some judgement about the extent to which non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of the law; Makes some reference to examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; Presents a structured response to the question using relevant legal terminology and concepts
6-10 marks: Demonstrates limited understanding of the law concerning families; Makes statements about how non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of the law; Makes limited reference to examples such as legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; Uses some relevant legal terminology
1-5 marks: Writes in general terms about the law concerning families; May include reference to legislation, cases, media, international instruments and documents; May refer to general legal terms

sampleAnswers.answer:
The statement is accurate to a considerable extent, although its force varies across the family law system. Family law provides strong legal tools to protect children and family members, but those tools depend on compliance by the people they bind. Where a parent or former partner refuses to comply with a court order, the protection that the law promises is weakened, and enforcement is often slow or incomplete.

The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) is the central statute. It requires courts to decide parenting matters according to the best interests of the child, and it requires most parties to attempt family dispute resolution before they go to court, with exceptions where there is family violence. Courts can make parenting orders about where children live and spend time, and the Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989 (Cth) sets how much a parent must pay. The law also protects family members from violence through state law. In New South Wales, the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) allows a court to make an apprehended domestic violence order, and breaching one is a criminal offence.

Non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of these tools in several ways. A parent who does not pay child support, or who withholds a child from the other parent in breach of a parenting order, may face enforcement that takes months, and the child may be harmed in the meantime. Breach of an apprehended domestic violence order is a criminal offence, yet victims may still be harmed before police can act, and some breaches are not reported. Enforcement depends on the victim making a complaint, and many victims do not do so because of fear, financial dependence or distrust of the process.

The law does respond to non-compliance. Courts can vary or enforce parenting orders and can make orders to remedy a breach, including compensation for costs caused by it. Child support can be recovered through the Services Australia child support system, which can act against a parent's income or other assets. Criminal penalties for breach of an apprehended domestic violence order send a clear message that breach is serious, and this deters some offenders.

Nevertheless, the law's effectiveness is not defeated by non-compliance, because many orders are complied with voluntarily and the system's design supports compliance. Family dispute resolution encourages parents to agree on arrangements rather than contest them, and the best interests principle keeps children's needs at the centre of decisions. The fact that breach is punishable gives the orders weight. Non-compliance affects a minority of cases, but the cases that fail are often the ones where the harm is greatest, which means the challenge to effectiveness is serious even if it is not widespread.

A contemporary issue is technology-facilitated abuse, in which a former partner uses phones, social media or tracking devices to monitor or threaten a family member. Such conduct can breach an apprehended domestic violence order, but the evidence is often digital and cross-jurisdictional, and police and courts may struggle to gather it quickly. This shows that the law's effectiveness depends on whether enforcement keeps pace with changing methods of non-compliance.

Overall, non-compliance challenges the effectiveness of family law, but the law can still deliver protection in most cases. Child support and parenting orders have enforcement mechanisms that work, though slowly, while family violence orders are effective only when breaches are reported and acted on. The statement is accurate to a considerable extent in relation to families, and the gap would narrow with faster enforcement, better access to evidence and greater support for victims to report breaches.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21-25 row by making an informed judgement that non-compliance challenges family law to a considerable extent, and by integrating the Family Law Act, child support and apprehended domestic violence orders as examples. Assessing the enforcement evidence more directly, such as how often breaches are reported, would sharpen the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The statement is partly accurate. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) gives courts power to make orders about children and property, and it requires the best interests of the child to be the main consideration. Courts can also make parenting orders and child support orders, and these protect families when people follow them.

However, not everyone follows family law orders. A parent may fail to pay child support or may refuse to let a child spend time with the other parent. These breaches are a problem because they can harm children and make it hard for the other parent to get on with their life. Courts can respond, but enforcement can be slow.

Family violence is a serious example. The Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) allows an apprehended domestic violence order to be made, and breaching the order is an offence. Many victims do not report breaches, so the law can only protect them if they come forward. Some people also find the process difficult to access, which means the law is less effective for them.

Overall, non-compliance does challenge the law, but the law still provides important protections for families. The statement is therefore accurate to some extent, because the effectiveness of family law depends on compliance, and where that fails, families are not protected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 11-15 row by making some judgement about whether non-compliance challenges family law, with some reference to the Family Law Act and to family violence orders. Explaining why enforcement fails in specific cases, rather than describing the orders, would lift it to the 16-20 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Family law in Australia is mainly in the Family Law Act 1975. It covers parenting, property and child support. Some people do not follow court orders, which means the law may not always work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-5 row by writing in general terms about family law without judging whether non-compliance challenges its effectiveness. Stating a position on the statement and naming one enforcement tool would lift it to the 6-10 row.

dotPoints.description: The responsibility of the state to protect families under international law

prompts.question: Explain the responsibility of the state to protect families under international law, using the scenario.
markerNotes: Explain the source of the obligation: a treaty, the nation that ratifies it, and how it becomes part of domestic law. Many students stop at the treaty without this final step.

The scenario tests the difference between an international obligation and domestic enforceability. A UN committee recommendation is not binding in the same way as legislation, and the answer should say so.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that Australia is bound by UN recommendations as if they were laws. Committee recommendations are influential but do not have the force of legislation.
Using 'the state' only to mean a state government. In international law the state is the nation, and its obligations are carried out by all levels of government.
keywords: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
Convention on the Rights of the Child
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains at least two sources of state responsibility under international law, such as the protection of families and children in the ICCPR and the CRC, explains that the treaties bind the nation and are not automatically part of domestic law, applies these points to the scenario, and identifies how domestic law gives effect to them
5 marks: Explains two sources accurately and applies at least one to the scenario, with reference to domestic implementation
4 marks: Explains two sources accurately, with limited application to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one source accurately
2 marks: Identifies a source with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that states must protect families

sampleAnswers.answer:
Under international law, the state has responsibility to protect families through the treaties it has ratified. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which Australia has ratified, recognises the family as the natural and fundamental group unit of society and entitles it to protection by society and the state (Article 23). The Convention on the Rights of the Child is more specific about children. It requires that the best interests of the child be a primary consideration in all actions concerning children (Article 3), and that the state provide appropriate assistance to parents in carrying out their responsibilities (Article 18).

These are obligations of the nation, not of any one government. However, Australia is a dualist country, so treaties are not automatically part of domestic law. In the scenario, the UN committee's recommendations reflect these responsibilities but are not binding in the same way as legislation. The obligations take effect in Australia through legislation and policy, such as the best interests principle in the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth). The state government would need to consider whether its laws and services already give effect to the treaties, rather than assuming the recommendations are enforceable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two treaties, the ICCPR and the Convention on the Rights of the Child, are explained with the specific provisions, and the answer distinguishes the nation's international responsibility from domestic enforceability. The UN recommendations in the scenario are applied to that distinction, which reaches the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ICCPR protects the family as a fundamental group unit, and the Convention on the Rights of the Child says the best interests of the child must be a primary consideration. Australia has ratified these treaties, so the national government has responsibilities under them. However, treaties do not automatically become part of Australian law, so the government must pass laws to put them into effect. The UN committee's recommendations in the scenario are not legally binding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two treaties are explained accurately, and the dualist point about domestic implementation is made. The application to the scenario is brief and the domestic implementation is not described in detail, so the answer is in the 4-mark band.

dotPoints.description: The role and impact of non-government organisations and the media in promoting and supporting families

prompts.question: Assess the role and impact of non-government organisations and the media in promoting and supporting families in Australia.
markerNotes: Assess needs a judgement about impact. Describe the roles briefly, then weigh them against criteria such as reach, accuracy, accessibility and independence.
The scenario gives two kinds of influence: services that give direct support, and public messages that shape attitudes. Top answers ask whether each one actually changes what families do.
Media coverage can raise awareness of family violence and encourage people to seek help, but sensational reporting can also harm families. A balanced answer names both sides.
commonStudentErrors: Describing services without assessing their impact on families.
Saying the media always helps families or always harms them, without weighing the evidence for either claim.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Assesses the role and impact of non-government organisations and the media in promoting and supporting families, weighs the benefits and limits of each against criteria such as reach, accuracy and access to services, and reaches a supported judgement about their overall impact
5-6 marks: Assesses the roles and impact of both non-government organisations and the media with reference to the scenario, reaching a partly supported conclusion, or explains their roles and some impact with limited judgement
4 marks: Describes the roles of non-government organisations or the media, with some explanation of impact and little assessment
2-3 marks: Identifies one role with minimal explanation, or describes a role of organisations or the media without assessment
1 mark: Makes a general statement about organisations and the media

sampleAnswers.answer: Non-government organisations and the media play important roles in promoting and supporting families, because they reach families in ways that government alone cannot. The scenario shows the first role clearly. The community organisation runs family support services, such as parenting programs and family dispute resolution, which give families direct support and help parents reach agreements without going to court. These services are often more accessible, more local and less formal than government services, which encourages families to seek help early. Their impact is significant because they can reduce the number of contested cases in the family courts and help children maintain relationships with both parents. However, their reach is limited by funding and by the number of places available, and they may not reach families in remote areas or those who do not speak English well. The second role is performed by the media. The newspaper series on family violence raises public awareness of the problem, explains the protection orders that are available and can encourage people experiencing violence to seek help. This is a powerful form of promoting families, because it changes how the community understands harm within families. However, media coverage can be selective or sensational, and it may risk identifying victims or focusing on individual cases in ways that distort the broader picture. The social media campaign encouraging mediation is a third form of influence. It can reach large numbers of people quickly and may change attitudes towards dispute resolution, but its impact depends on whether people act on it, and that is difficult to measure. Weighing these roles against the criteria of reach, accuracy, accessibility and independence, non-government organisations have the strongest direct impact on families, because they provide services. The media has the widest reach, but its impact is less predictable and cannot be targeted to individual families in need. In my judgement, the combination of direct services and public awareness has a positive overall impact, but it depends on the services being adequately funded and on the media coverage being responsible.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Non-government services and media coverage are each assessed against the criteria of reach, accessibility, accuracy and targeting, and the social media campaign is weighed for its measurable impact. The answer reaches a supported judgement that the combination has a positive but conditional impact, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Non-government organisations and the media both help families. The community organisation in the scenario runs parenting programs and dispute resolution, which help families avoid court. The newspaper series raises public awareness of family violence and explains protection orders, so people may seek help. The social media campaign encourages mediation. However, the media can be sensational, and services depend on funding. Overall, I think they have a positive impact on families, although their reach is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The roles of both organisations and the media are explained and their impact is noted, with a limits point and a brief judgement. The criteria are not set out and the assessment is limited, so the answer is in the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The community organisation runs parenting programs. The newspaper reports on family violence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two roles are identified with minimal explanation and no assessment. This is the 2-mark band.

dotPoints.description: Types of family structures, including the interconnections of kinship, Community and shared responsibilities for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

prompts.question: Describe the types of family structures in Australia, including the structures of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
markerNotes: Describe the structures and what they involve, not only their legal status. Full marks show how the structures work in practice, particularly for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families.
Describe kinship with care. It is a system of relationships and obligations, and it extends well beyond the household.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander family structures as simply extended families, which misses the kinship and community obligations involved.
Presenting the nuclear family as the normal model, with other structures treated as exceptions.

2 marks: Describes two family structures in general terms

sampleAnswers.answer: Australian family structures include nuclear families with two parents, single-parent families with one parent, and blended families that combine children from earlier relationships. Same-sex parent families have two parents of the same sex. The family structures of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are often built around kinship, a network of family ties and obligations extending to grandparents, aunts and uncles. Children are cared for by this network, so these shared responsibilities extend across the extended family and community, and a child's family is not always their household.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Four family structures are described, and the kinship, community and shared responsibilities of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families are explained in terms of how they operate, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nuclear family has two parents and their children, and a single-parent family has one parent and children.
